claims.claim: Money is defined functionally as whatever people regularly use and widely accept when buying and selling goods and services; it is defined by what it does, not by what it is made of.

Money performs three core functions: a medium of exchange (an intermediary between buyer and seller), a unit of account (a common measure for quoting prices, debts, and wealth), and a store of value (holding purchasing power over time). Some textbooks add a fourth, a standard of deferred payment.

Barter requires a double coincidence of wants — each trader must want exactly what the other offers — which makes many trades impossible; because a medium of exchange is accepted by everyone, a seller can accept money from anyone and spend it with anyone, removing the double-coincidence requirement.

Commodity money is a good with intrinsic value that also circulates as money (gold, silver, cowrie shells, cigarettes, cocoa beans); commodity-backed currency is paper redeemable for a commodity such as gold; fiat money has no intrinsic value and is declared by a government to be legal tender. Modern U.S. currency is fiat money and states that it is 'legal tender for all debts, public and private.'

M1 is the narrowest common money measure and consists of currency held by the public (outside the U.S. Treasury, the Federal Reserve, and depository institutions), demand deposits, and other liquid deposits (which include savings/money-market deposit accounts).

M2 equals M1 plus (1) small-denomination time deposits (amounts under $100,000) and (2) balances in retail money-market funds, less IRA and Keogh balances at depository institutions and money-market funds. Because M2 contains all of M1, M2 is always at least as large as M1.

Beginning with the May 2020 data, savings deposits were reclassified from M2-only into M1: after the Board removed the six-per-month transfer limit on savings accounts in Regulation D (interim final rule, April 24, 2020), savings deposits gained the liquidity of transaction accounts and were combined with other checkable deposits into 'other liquid deposits' within M1. This raised measured M1 by approximately $11 trillion (the industry total of savings deposits was about $11.2 trillion).

The store-of-value function depends on relatively stable purchasing power; sustained inflation, by reducing what each unit of money buys, erodes money's ability to store value (developed in full by the inflation topic).

Worked example (independently computed): $200 cash + $1,500 checking + $6,000 savings = $7,700 in M1; adding a $5,000 small-denomination certificate of deposit gives $12,700 in M2. The CD is in M2 but not M1.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Number of functions of money (three vs four)
positions: Many textbooks list three functions: medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value
Some texts, including OpenStax, also list a fourth, a standard of deferred payment
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the three core functions the topic owns and notes the sometimes-added fourth function in one parenthetical, without over-claiming a single canonical count.

unsupportedExistingClaims: No prior published draft for this topic existed in lessons.json for review (economics is a fresh phase-4 subject); the lesson was written from verified sources, not corrected from generated boilerplate.
correctionsNeeded: Used the current Federal Reserve H.6 definition of M1, which since May 2020 includes savings deposits under 'other liquid deposits' — an easy point to get wrong from pre-2020 textbook memory; the change is dated and attributed to the Fed.
Kept the topic within its boundary: bank money creation, the Fed, monetary policy, and inflation mechanics are named and handed off rather than taught.
